title: pranayama sequences
hook: a hatha yoga manual compares the breath to a lion, an elephant and a tiger

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gita's line: in-breath offered into out-breath, each step handed to the next. Breath offered into breath.

A lion, an elephant and a tiger: not the usual cast for a breathing lesson. They turn up in the second chapter of the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, a manual for yogis, right where it starts teaching breath. Nobody walks up to a wild lion on the first day and puts a hand on its head. Taming one goes slowly, a little closer each day. The breath, the text says, is like that. Then it adds a warning that isn't gentle at all.
screen: `A LION, AN ELEPHANT, A TIGER.` → `TAMED A LITTLE AT A TIME.` → `THE BREATH IS LIKE THAT.`

segments.voice: Chapter two, verse fifteen, in paraphrase: as a lion, an elephant or a tiger is brought under control slowly, little by little, so the breath is brought under control. Otherwise, it harms the one who practices. The next verse adds that breath practice done properly helps, and done wrongly brings illness. That's striking from a book that loves breath practice. It isn't warning people off; it's warning them about order. Teachers have a Sanskrit word for the idea, though the verse doesn't use it: krama, a step, going in order. A sequence isn't only a list. It's a decision about what comes first and what has to wait. A few verses earlier, the chapter gives the reason breath matters at all: when the breath moves unsteadily, the mind is unsteady; when the breath is still, the mind is still. The breath is a way in to the mind, so the manual treats it the way a keeper treats a big animal. Some teachers in the hatha tradition begin with slow breathing and simple counting, and leave long holds for later, sometimes learned one to one with someone watching. This week has followed that line: the breath the others rise with, the seat before the breath, breath offered into breath, and now the pace. The week began with the Ashtavakra Gita, a text about a self already free, and the two pull in different directions. At one point the sage tells Janaka that practicing meditation is itself his bondage; the hatha manual is practice from start to finish. The tradition has kept both books, and some teachers read both.
screen: `TAMED LITTLE BY LITTLE.` · `DONE WRONGLY, IT HARMS.` · `UNSTEADY BREATH, UNSTEADY MIND.` · `GENTLE FIRST, LONG HOLDS LATER.`

segments.voice: Start with a few breaths as they come, then a gentle count: in for four, out for four. When that's easy, stretch only the out-breath to five or six, and if the chest, throat or jaw strains, return to the even count; that return is part of the sequence, not a failure of it. Near the end, drop the counting and let the breath settle by itself.
Pranayama sequences. Breath practices set in an order. Today, the pace of that order: little by little, the way a keeper tames a lion.
Your line: little by little. The keeper doesn't rush the lion, and neither does the manual. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In some hatha yoga lineages, breath practices are learned in order, gentle ones first, with longer holds left until later and sometimes taught one to one by a teacher who watches the student.
